at jage.explanation: "At jage" means "to hunt or chase". To say someone runs after a person to catch them, use it for the chase: "Politiet jager tyven" (The police chase the thief). To say someone hunts wild animals, use it for the hunt: "Han jager hjorte" (He hunts deer).

sentence.da: Hunden vil **jage** katten ud af haven.
sentence.en: The dog wants to chase the cat out of the garden.

at jamre.explanation: "At jamre" means "to wail or whine". To say what someone complains about, put "over" (about) after it: "Han jamrer over vejret" (He whines about the weather).

sentence.da: Hun bliver ved med at **jamre** over, at det regner.
sentence.en: She keeps whining that it is raining.

at juble.explanation: "At juble" means "to cheer". It is the verb for the noun "en jubel" (jubilation). To say when people cheer, add a sentence with "når" (when): "Folk jubler, når holdet scorer" (People cheer when the team scores).

sentence.da: Publikum begynder at **juble**, når sangeren kommer ind.
sentence.en: The audience starts to cheer when the singer comes in.

at justere.explanation: "At justere" means "to adjust". Do not copy the "ad" of "adjust": the Danish word starts with "ju". To say you change a plan a little, put the plan after it: "Vi justerer planen" (We are adjusting the plan).

sentence.da: Mekanikeren vil **justere** bremserne, fordi de er for løse.
sentence.en: The mechanic wants to adjust the brakes because they are too loose.

en jagt.explanation: "En jagt" means "a hunt". It is the noun for the verb "at jage" (to chase). To talk about looking hard for something, use "jagten på" (the hunt for): "jagten på en bolig" (the hunt for a home).

sentence.da: Mange danskere går på **jagt** efter hjorte om efteråret.
sentence.en: Many Danes go hunting for deer in the fall.

en jakke.explanation: "En jakke" means "a jacket". To talk about a long, warm coat instead, use "en frakke" (a coat): "Jeg tager frakken på" (I put my coat on).

sentence.da: Tag din **jakke** på i kulden.
sentence.en: Put your jacket on in the cold.

en japaner.explanation: "En japaner" means "a Japanese person". To describe things from Japan, use "japansk" (Japanese) instead: "japansk te" (Japanese tea).

sentence.da: Min ven er **japaner**, og han bor i Tokyo.
sentence.en: My friend is Japanese, and he lives in Tokyo.

en jobannonce.explanation: "En jobannonce" means "a job ad". It is built from "job" (job) and "en annonce" (an ad).

sentence.da: I en **jobannonce** står der, hvilke opgaver du skal løse.
sentence.en: A job ad says which tasks you will do.

en jobsamtale.explanation: "En jobsamtale" means "a job interview". It is built from "job" (job) and "en samtale" (a conversation). To say you are going to one, use "til" (to): "Jeg skal til jobsamtale" (I am going to a job interview).

sentence.da: Jeg har en **jobsamtale** i morgen og er nervøs.
sentence.en: I have a job interview tomorrow and am nervous.

en joke.explanation: "En joke" means "a joke". To say you tell one, use "at fortælle" (to tell): "Han fortæller en joke" (He tells a joke). To say you are not serious, use "at lave sjov" (to kid around): "Jeg laver bare sjov" (I am just joking).

sentence.da: Hans **joke** fik os alle til at grine.
sentence.en: His joke made us all laugh.

en jomfru.explanation: "En jomfru" means "a virgin or maiden". To name the mother of Jesus, use it in "Jomfru Maria" (the Virgin Mary). To name the star sign, use "Jomfruen" (Virgo).

sentence.da: I eventyret redder ridderen den smukke **jomfru** fra tårnet.
sentence.en: In the fairy tale the knight saves the beautiful maiden from the tower.

en jordemoder.explanation: "En jordemoder" means "a midwife". It is built from "jord" (earth) and "moder" (mother). In Denmark, a "jordemoder" leads a normal birth, and a doctor joins only if there are problems.

sentence.da: En **jordemoder** hjælper kvinden, mens hun føder.
sentence.en: A midwife helps the woman while she gives birth.

en jordnød.explanation: "En jordnød" means "a peanut". It is built from "jord" (ground) and "en nød" (a nut).

sentence.da: Jeg åbner skallen og spiser en **jordnød**.
sentence.en: I open the shell and eat a peanut.

en journal.explanation: "En journal" means "a medical record". To say a diary instead, use "en dagbog" (a diary): "Jeg skriver i min dagbog" (I write in my diary).

sentence.da: Lægen skriver i din **journal**, hvilken medicin du har fået.
sentence.en: The doctor writes in your medical record which medicine you have gotten.

en journalist.explanation: "En journalist" means "a journalist". To name the job, put "som" (as) before it: "Hun arbejder som journalist" (She works as a journalist).

sentence.da: En **journalist** skriver om nyheder i avisen.
sentence.en: A journalist writes about news in the paper.

en juleferie.explanation: "En juleferie" means "a Christmas vacation". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "ferie" (vacation). To say you are on vacation, use "ferie" as its own word: "Jeg har ferie" (I am on vacation).

sentence.da: Vi skal have en lang **juleferie** sammen med familien.
sentence.en: We are going to have a long Christmas vacation together with the family.

en julefrokost.explanation: "En julefrokost" means "a Christmas lunch". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "frokost" (lunch). In Denmark, a "julefrokost" is a big get-together in December with food and drinks.

sentence.da: Vi har **julefrokost** med kollegerne i december.
sentence.en: We have a Christmas lunch with our coworkers in December.

en julegave.explanation: "En julegave" means "a Christmas present". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "en gave" (a gift). To thank someone for any gift, use "gave" as its own word: "Tak for gaven!" (Thanks for the gift!)

sentence.da: Under juletræet ligger en **julegave** til dig.
sentence.en: Under the Christmas tree there is a Christmas present for you.

en julemand.explanation: "En julemand" means "a Santa Claus". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "mand" (man). To make other Christmas words, put "jul" in front: "et julekort" (a Christmas card).

sentence.da: Far er klædt ud som **julemand** i dag.
sentence.en: Dad is dressed up as Santa Claus today.

en julemiddag.explanation: "En julemiddag" means "a Christmas dinner". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "middag" (dinner). To talk about a Christmas lunch party instead, use "en julefrokost" (a Christmas lunch): "Vi har julefrokost på arbejdet" (We have a Christmas lunch at work).

sentence.da: Vi spiser **julemiddag** hos min mormor.
sentence.en: We eat Christmas dinner at my grandmother's.

en julesang.explanation: "En julesang" means "a Christmas carol". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "sang" (song). The part "sang" also appears in "en børnesang" (a children's song).

sentence.da: Vi synger altid en **julesang** ved juletræet.
sentence.en: We always sing a Christmas carol at the Christmas tree.

en julestjerne.explanation: "En julestjerne" means "a poinsettia". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "en stjerne" (a star). To talk about a star decoration, it also means "a Christmas star": "Vi hænger en julestjerne op i vinduet" (We hang a Christmas star in the window).

sentence.da: I december står der en rød **julestjerne** i vinduet i stuen.
sentence.en: In December a red poinsettia stands in the living room window.

en jungle.explanation: "En jungle" means "a jungle". To talk about a confusing mess of things, use it as a picture: "en jungle af regler" (a jungle of rules).

sentence.da: Tigeren bor i en tæt **jungle**.
sentence.en: The tiger lives in a dense jungle.

en jurist.explanation: "En jurist" means "a legal professional". It comes from "jura" (law as a subject). To name the person who argues a case in court, use "en advokat" (a lawyer): "Jeg ringer til en advokat" (I am calling a lawyer).

sentence.da: Han er uddannet **jurist** og arbejder i et ministerium.
sentence.en: He is a trained legal professional and works in a ministry.

en jury.explanation: "En jury" means "a jury". To say a person is a member, use "sidde i" (to sit in): "Hun sidder i juryen" (She is on the jury).

sentence.da: I tv-programmet giver en **jury** point til hver deltager.
sentence.en: In the TV show a jury gives points to each contestant.

en jyde.explanation: "En jyde" means "a Jutlander". It comes from "Jylland" (Jutland), the part of Denmark that is connected to Germany. The dialect of Jutland is called "jysk" (Jutlandic).

sentence.da: Min nabo er **jyde** og kommer fra Aalborg.
sentence.en: My neighbor is a Jutlander and comes from Aalborg.

en jæger.explanation: "En jæger" means "a hunter". In Denmark, a hunter must have "et jagttegn" (a hunting license).

sentence.da: En **jæger** skyder hjorte og fasaner i skoven.
sentence.en: A hunter shoots deer and pheasants in the forest.

sentence.da: I de gamle nordiske sagn bor der en **jætte** i bjerget.
sentence.en: In the old Norse legends a giant lives in the mountain.

en jøde.explanation: "En jøde" means "a Jew". To say Jewish, use "jødisk" (Jewish) instead: "jødisk mad" (Jewish food).

sentence.da: Min ven er **jøde** og går i synagoge om lørdagen.
sentence.en: My friend is Jewish and goes to synagogue on Saturdays.

et jakkesæt.explanation: "Et jakkesæt" means "a suit". It is built from "jakke" (jacket) and "sæt" (set). To talk about things that belong together, use "et sæt" (a set): "et sæt bestik" (a set of silverware).

sentence.da: Mange mænd har et **jakkesæt** på til et bryllup.
sentence.en: Many men wear a suit to a wedding.

et job.explanation: "Et job" means "a job". To say you got a new position, say: "Jeg har et nyt job" (I have a new job). To say you are going to the place where you work, use "arbejde" (work) instead: "Jeg skal på arbejde" (I am going to work).

sentence.da: Jeg kan lide mit **job** på kontoret.
sentence.en: I like my job at the office.

et jobcenter.explanation: "Et jobcenter" means "a job center". In Denmark, a "jobcenter" is run by the local council and helps people without work find a job and get financial support.

sentence.da: Kommunens **jobcenter** hjælper folk uden arbejde med at finde et nyt.
sentence.en: The municipality's job center helps people without work find a new one.

et jordbær.explanation: "Et jordbær" means "a strawberry". It is built from "jord" (earth, ground) and "et bær" (a berry). To talk about soil, use "jord" as its own word: "Planten står i jord" (The plant is in the soil).

sentence.da: Om sommeren spiser vi **jordbær** med fløde.
sentence.en: In the summer we eat strawberries with cream.

et jordskælv.explanation: "Et jordskælv" means "an earthquake". It is built from "jord" (earth) and "skælv" (a tremble). To say a person trembles, use the verb "at skælve" (to tremble): "Han skælver af kulde" (He trembles from cold).

sentence.da: Husene faldt sammen efter et **jordskælv**.
sentence.en: The houses collapsed after an earthquake.

et jubilæum.explanation: "Et jubilæum" means "an anniversary". To name a round number of years for a club, use it with the number: "Klubben har 50-års jubilæum" (The club has its 50-year anniversary). To name a couple's wedding anniversary, use "en bryllupsdag" (a wedding anniversary) instead: "I dag er det vores bryllupsdag" (Today is our wedding anniversary).

sentence.da: Firmaet fejrer sit 25-års **jubilæum** med en stor fest.
sentence.en: The company is celebrating its 25th anniversary with a big party.

et julesalg.explanation: "Et julesalg" means "a Christmas sale". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "salg" (sale).

sentence.da: I december har mange butikker **julesalg**.
sentence.en: In December, many shops have a Christmas sale.

et juletræ.explanation: "Et juletræ" means "a Christmas tree". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "et træ" (a tree). To make other Christmas words, put "jul" in front: "et julekort" (a Christmas card).

sentence.da: Vi pynter et **juletræ** med lys og kugler.
sentence.en: We decorate a Christmas tree with lights and ornaments.

ja.explanation: "Ja" means "yes". To accept an offer politely, add "tak" (thanks): "Ja, tak" (Yes, please). To answer yes to a question that has "ikke" (not) in it, say "jo" (yes) instead: "Kommer du ikke?" "Jo." (Aren't you coming? Yes, I am.)

sentence.da: Vil du have kaffe? **Ja**, tak.
sentence.en: Do you want coffee? Yes, please.

jalousi.explanation: "Jalousi" means "jealousy". English speakers should note the spelling: it has no "e" and ends in "i". The describing word is "jaloux" (jealous): "Han er jaloux" (He is jealous).

sentence.da: **Jalousi** kan ødelægge et godt forhold.
sentence.en: Jealousy can ruin a good relationship.

jaloux.explanation: "Jaloux" means "jealous". To name the person you are jealous of, put "på" (of) after it: "Hun er jaloux på sin kollega" (She is jealous of her coworker).

sentence.da: Han er **jaloux** på sin bror.
sentence.en: He is jealous of his brother.

jaloux på.explanation: "Jaloux på" means "jealous of". To say you want what someone has, say: "Jeg er jaloux på din nye bil" (I am jealous of your new car). To say you fear someone will take a person you love, say: "Han er jaloux på hendes ven" (He is jealous of her friend).

forms.da: Hun er jaloux på sin søster.
forms.en: She is jealous of her sister.

sentence.da: Han er **jaloux på** min nye cykel.
sentence.en: He is jealous of my new bike.

jamen.explanation: "Jamen" means "but". To object to what someone said, start your reply with it: "Jamen, det passer ikke!" (But that is not true!) To ask why something is not so, it means "well": "Jamen, hvorfor ikke?" (Well, why not?)

sentence.da: **Jamen**, det var slet ikke min idé!
sentence.en: But that was not my idea at all!

januar.explanation: "Januar" means "January". To say in which month something happens, use "i" (in): "Jeg har fødselsdag i januar" (My birthday is in January). English speakers should spell it with no "y" at the end.

sentence.da: Det er koldt i **januar**.
sentence.en: It is cold in January.

japan.explanation: "Japan" means "Japan". To describe things from Japan, use "japansk" (Japanese) instead: "japansk te" (Japanese tea).

sentence.da: Sushi kommer fra **Japan**.
sentence.en: Sushi comes from Japan.

japansk.explanation: "Japansk" means "Japanese". It comes from "Japan" (Japan). To name the language, use it as the language: "Jeg taler japansk" (I speak Japanese).

sentence.da: Sushi er **japansk** mad.
sentence.en: Sushi is Japanese food.

jaså.explanation: "Jaså" means "is that so". To answer news that surprises you, say it as your reply: "Jeg har købt en hund." "Jaså!" (I have bought a dog. Is that so!)

forms.en: Oh, I did not know that.

sentence.da: Du har fået nyt job? **Jaså**, det er flot.
sentence.en: You have a new job? Is that so? That is great.

javel.explanation: "Javel" means "I see". To show you have heard what someone said, say it as your reply: "Jeg er flyttet." "Javel." (I have moved. I see.)

sentence.da: Du kommer for sent? **Javel**.
sentence.en: You are coming late? I see.

jazz.explanation: "Jazz" means "jazz music". To say you like it, use it without an article: "Jeg kan godt lide jazz" (I like jazz).

sentence.da: Han spiller **jazz** på sin saxofon.
sentence.en: He plays jazz on his saxophone.

jeg.explanation: "Jeg" means "I". To say who does something, use "jeg": "Jeg ser ham" (I see him). To say who it happens to, use "mig" (me): "Han ser mig" (He sees me).

sentence.da: **Jeg** bor i København.
sentence.en: I live in Copenhagen.

jeg beklager.explanation: "Jeg beklager" means "sorry". It is the formal way to apologize, as in "Jeg beklager forsinkelsen" (I am sorry for the delay). For a quick sorry, like bumping into someone, say "undskyld" (sorry): "Undskyld, jeg ramte dig" (Sorry, I bumped into you).

sentence.da: Det er min fejl, og **jeg beklager**.
sentence.en: It is my mistake, and I apologize.

jeg er enig.explanation: "Jeg er enig" means "I agree". "Enig" means "in agreement", so it literally says "I am in agreement". To name the person you agree with, add "med" (with): "Jeg er enig med dig" (I agree with you).

sentence.da: **Jeg er enig** med dig.
sentence.en: I agree with you.

jeg er ked af det.explanation: "Jeg er ked af det" means "I'm sad". When you regret something you did, it also means "I'm sorry": "Jeg er ked af det, jeg glemte din fødselsdag" (I'm sorry, I forgot your birthday). For a quick apology, like bumping into someone, say "undskyld" (sorry): "Undskyld, jeg ramte dig" (Sorry, I bumped into you).

sentence.da: Undskyld, **jeg er ked af det**.
sentence.en: Sorry, I feel bad about it.

jeg er uenig.explanation: "Jeg er uenig" means "I disagree". To say who you disagree with, add "med" (with): "Jeg er uenig med dig" (I disagree with you). To name the topic, add "i" (in): "Vi er uenige i det" (We disagree about that).

sentence.da: **Jeg er uenig**, men jeg forstår dig.
sentence.en: I disagree, but I understand you.

jeg forstår ikke.explanation: "Jeg forstår ikke" means "I don't understand". It is built from "forstår" (understand) and "ikke" (not). To say "I don't understand it", put "det" (it) before "ikke": "Jeg forstår det ikke". To ask someone to say it again, add: "Kan du gentage det?" (Can you repeat that?).

sentence.da: Undskyld, **jeg forstår ikke**.
sentence.en: Sorry, I don't understand.

jeg glæder mig.explanation: "Jeg glæder mig" means "I'm looking forward to it". It literally says "I gladden myself", with "mig" (myself). To name what you look forward to, add "til" (to): "Jeg glæder mig til ferien" (I'm looking forward to the vacation).

forms.en: I'm looking forward to the weekend.
We're looking forward to the party.

sentence.da: **Jeg glæder mig** meget til sommeren.
sentence.en: I'm really looking forward to summer.

jeg har det godt.explanation: "Jeg har det godt" means "I'm doing well". It literally says "I have it good", with "det" (it) after "har". To answer "Hvordan har du det?" (How are you?), say: "Jeg har det godt" (I'm doing well).

sentence.da: Tak, **jeg har det godt**. Og dig?
sentence.en: Thanks, I'm doing well. And you?

jeg har det skidt.explanation: "Jeg har det skidt" means "I'm not doing well". It literally says "I have it badly", with "skidt" (badly). To say it more gently, say: "Jeg har det ikke så godt" (I'm not doing so well).

sentence.da: Jeg er syg. **Jeg har det skidt**.
sentence.en: I am sick. I'm not doing well.

jeg hedder….explanation: "Jeg hedder…" means "my name is…" and you add your name after it. It literally says "I am called…", from "at hedde" (to be called). To answer, the other person can say "Dejligt at møde dig" (Nice to meet you).

forms.da: Hvad hedder du? Jeg hedder Lars.

sentence.da: **Jeg hedder** Anna, og du?
sentence.en: My name is Anna. And you?

jeg kommer fra….explanation: "Jeg kommer fra…" means "I'm from…" and you add a country or town after it. It literally says "I come from…". To answer "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?), say: "Jeg kommer fra Danmark" (I'm from Denmark).

sentence.da: **Jeg kommer fra** Canada.
sentence.en: I'm from Canada.

jeg vil gerne have.explanation: "Jeg vil gerne have" means "I would like". To order or ask for something politely, name the item after "have": "Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe" (I would like a coffee). Without "gerne" (gladly), "Jeg vil have en kaffe" (I want a coffee) is blunt.

forms.da: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe.
Jeg vil gerne have to billetter.

sentence.da: **Jeg vil gerne have** en kop te.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of tea.

jer.explanation: "Jer" means "you" when you talk to several people and something is done to them: "Jeg kan se jer" (I can see you all). For several people doing something, Danish uses "I": "I er søde" (You are all nice). For one person, use "dig" (you): "Jeg kan se dig" (I can see you).

sentence.da: Børn, jeg har en gave til **jer**.
sentence.en: Children, I have a gift for you all.

jeres.explanation: "Jeres" means "your" when you talk to several people: "jeres bil" (your car, a group). For one person, use "din" (your): "din bil" (your car, one person). Use "jeres" before every kind of word: "jeres hus" (your house), "jeres børn" (your children).

sentence.da: Mor og far, er det **jeres** bil?
sentence.en: Mom and Dad, is that your car?

jern.explanation: "Jern" means "iron", as in the metal. To talk about the mineral in food, use the same word: "Spinat indeholder jern" (Spinach contains iron). "En jernbane" (a railway) is built from "jern" and "bane" (track).

sentence.da: Gelænderet er lavet af **jern**.
sentence.en: The railing is made of iron.

jetlag.explanation: "Jetlag" means "jet lag". Danish writes it as one word, "jetlag", where English writes two words.

forms.en: We got jet lag in Tokyo
How do you get over jet lag?

sentence.da: Efter flyveturen havde jeg **jetlag** i to dage.
sentence.en: After the flight I had jet lag for two days.

jo.explanation: "Jo" means "yes" when you answer a question that has "ikke" (not) in it, and "you know" in the middle of a sentence. When someone asks "Har du ikke spist?" (Haven't you eaten?), you answer "Jo, det har jeg" (Yes, I have). When you mention something the other person already knows, put "jo" inside the sentence: "Det er jo min bil" (It is my car, you know). For a yes to a question without "ikke", use "ja" (yes): "Kommer du?" "Ja!" (Are you coming? Yes!)

sentence.da: Kommer du ikke? **Jo**, jeg kommer!
sentence.en: Aren't you coming? Yes, I am!

jo ... desto.explanation: "Jo ... desto" means "the ... the", for two things that grow together. "Jo" starts the first part and "desto" starts the second: "Jo mere du øver, desto hurtigere bliver du" (The more you practice, the faster you get).

forms.da: Jo mere du øver, desto bedre bliver du
forms.en: The more you practice, the better you get

sentence.da: **Jo** ældre han bliver, **desto** mere sover han.
sentence.en: The older he gets, the more he sleeps.

jord.explanation: "Jord" means "earth or soil". To talk about a piece of land, use it with "et stykke" (a piece): "et stykke jord" (a plot of land).

sentence.da: Planter har brug for vand og **jord**.
sentence.en: Plants need water and soil.

jubel.explanation: "Jubel" means "cheering". It is the noun for the verb "at juble" (to cheer).

forms.en: There was jubilation in the hall

sentence.da: Efter målet brød der **jubel** ud på tribunen.
sentence.en: After the goal, cheering broke out in the stands.

juice.explanation: "Juice" means "juice". To name the fruit, put it in front of "juice", as in "appelsinjuice" (orange juice) or "æblejuice" (apple juice).

related.en: fruit cordial (a sweet syrup mixed with water)

sentence.da: Man laver **juice** af appelsiner.
sentence.en: You make juice from oranges.

jul.explanation: "Jul" means "Christmas". To say when something happens, use "til jul" (at Christmas): "Vi ses til jul" (See you at Christmas). To talk about the whole season, use "i julen" (during the Christmas season): "Jeg læser meget i julen" (I read a lot during the Christmas season).

sentence.da: Vi får gaver til **jul**.
sentence.en: We get presents at Christmas.

juleaften.explanation: "Juleaften" means "Christmas Eve". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "aften" (evening). To say today is that evening, use it without an article: "Det er juleaften i dag" (It is Christmas Eve today).

sentence.da: På **juleaften** pynter vi juletræet og får gaver.
sentence.en: On Christmas Eve we decorate the Christmas tree and get presents.

julepynt.explanation: "Julepynt" means "Christmas decorations". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "pynt" (decoration). To say you put them up, use it without an article: "Vi hænger julepynt op" (We hang up Christmas decorations).

sentence.da: **Julepynt** er kugler og stjerner til juletræet.
sentence.en: Christmas decorations are balls and stars for the Christmas tree.

juli.explanation: "Juli" means "July". Unlike English, Danish spells month names like ordinary words, so you write "i juli" (in July), not "i Juli".

sentence.da: Efter juni kommer **juli**.
sentence.en: After June comes July.

juni.explanation: "Juni" means "June". Unlike English, Danish spells month names like ordinary words, so you write "i juni" (in June), not "i Juni".

sentence.da: Det er lyst længe i **juni**.
sentence.en: It stays light for a long time in June.

jura.explanation: "Jura" means "law", as the subject you study at university: "Hun læser jura på universitetet" (She studies law at the university). To talk about one rule made by the state, use "en lov" (a law): "Det er en ny lov" (It is a new law).

sentence.da: Hun læser **jura** for at blive advokat.
sentence.en: She studies law to become a lawyer.

juridisk.explanation: "Juridisk" means "legal", in the sense of law and courts. To call something a legal matter, say: "Det er et juridisk problem, ikke et politisk" (It is a legal problem, not a political one). Do not mix it up with "lovlig" (allowed by law): "Det er lovligt at parkere her" (It is legal to park here).

sentence.da: En advokat kan give dig **juridisk** hjælp med kontrakten.
sentence.en: A lawyer can give you legal help with the contract.

jysk.explanation: "Jysk" means "Jutlandic", from or about "Jylland" (Jutland), the part of Denmark that is joined to the rest of Europe. To talk about the way people speak there, use it as the name of the dialect: "Jeg forstår ikke jysk" (I do not understand Jutlandic).

sentence.da: Min mormor fra Aalborg taler **jysk**.
sentence.en: My grandmother from Aalborg speaks Jutlandic.

jævnligt.explanation: "Jævnligt" means "regularly". It comes from "jævn" (even). Its opposite is "sjældent" (rarely): "Jeg ser ham sjældent" (I rarely see him).

sentence.da: Jeg går **jævnligt** ture for at holde mig i form.
sentence.en: I go for walks regularly to stay in shape.

jødedom.explanation: "Jødedom" means "Judaism". It is built from "jøde" (Jew) and "-dom". The ending "-dom" is also in "barndom" (childhood) and "kristendom" (Christianity).

sentence.da: Han har læst meget om **jødedom** og dens historie.
sentence.en: He has read a lot about Judaism and its history.

jødisk.explanation: "Jødisk" means "Jewish". It comes from "en jøde" (a Jew). To name the religion, use "jødedom" (Judaism): "Han studerer jødedom" (He studies Judaism).

sentence.da: Min ven er **jødisk** og fejrer Hanukkah i december.
sentence.en: My friend is Jewish and celebrates Hanukkah in December.

jøsses.explanation: "Jøsses" means "gosh". It is a mild exclamation, so it is not rude. To react to surprising news: "Jeg har vundet i lotteriet!" "Jøsses!" (I won the lottery! Gosh!)

sentence.da: **Jøsses**, hvor er der mange mennesker her!
sentence.en: Gosh, there are so many people here!
